extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, labor and employment attorneys, labor advocates, and DOL enforcement staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the FLSA economic-realities test to determine whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor, focusing here on the investments factor and the degree of permanence of the work relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investments factor (§ 795.110(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the worker's investments support an independent business or serve a business-like function; worker investments that are capital in nature (i.e., allow the worker to do more work and extend market reach) indicate independent contractor status, while relatively minor investments that do little to further a business indicate employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both the nature and effect of the investment (not merely dollar amount). Personal-use property (e.g., a personal vehicle used without modification) ordinarily is not a capital or entrepreneurial investment. Compare the types of investments made by the worker with those made by the potential employer to determine whether the worker is making similar types of investments (even if on a smaller scale) that allow the worker to operate independently. The Department cites case law and prior guidance supporting comparison of worker and employer investments and emphasizes focusing on qualitative characteristics of investments rather than strictly quantitative measures. Example scenarios provided: (1) a graphic designer who only occasionally uses preferred drafting tools while the firm provides software/computer/office — minor investment that indicates employee status; (2) a graphic designer who purchases design software, computer, rents office space, and markets their services — investments that support an independent business and indicate independent contractor status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative investments — qualitative (not solely quantitative) comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The worker's investments need not be equal to the potential employer's investments and should not be compared only in terms of dollar values or business size; instead, focus on whether the worker is making similar types of investments as the potential employer that suggest the worker can operate independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modification addresses concerns that mere size or dollar comparisons would unfairly favor employers. Courts of appeals have routinely compared relative investments, but the Department instructs that qualitative similarity of investment types (even on a smaller scale) is the better indicator of whether a worker is in business for themself. This approach aims to avoid excluding sole proprietors or smaller-scale businesses from independent-contractor status solely because they invest less money than larger employers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of Permanence of the Work Relationship (§ 795.110(b)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the work relationship is indefinite/continuous or definite/non-exclusive/project-based/sporadic; an indefinite or continuous relationship (or exclusivity) often weighs in favor of employee status, while definite-duration, non-exclusive, project-based, or sporadic relationships often weigh toward independent contractor status — but lack of permanence alone is not dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether lack of permanence results from the worker's own independent business initiative or from operational characteristics intrinsic to the industry or business; if lack of permanence is due to industry operational characteristics (e.g., seasonal or temporary demand) and not the worker's independent business initiative, it is not necessarily indicative of independent contractor status unless the worker is exercising independent business initiative. Recognize that independent contractors can have regularly occurring fixed periods of work and long-term clients; project-based work alone is not determinative. Exclusivity of the relationship is appropriately considered under the permanence factor (and may also be considered under the control factor where it reflects employer control). Contractual renewals that are routine or automatic indicate permanence and an indefinite working arrangement associated with employment. Example: a cook who provides meals continuously and exclusively for a venue, prepares meals as directed, and has a high degree of permanence and exclusivity — facts that indicate employee status under the permanence factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity and multiple factors — how to weigh facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts such as exclusivity, long-term repeated relationships, or working for multiple entities must be considered in context; exclusivity can indicate permanence/employee status, but exclusivity alone is not determinative and may also reflect employer control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat exclusivity or long-term relationships as automatically dispositive. Courts have considered exclusivity under both permanence and control; an exclusive relationship is a hallmark of many employment relationships but independent contractors may also have exclusive or long-term clients. Similarly, working for multiple employers does not automatically indicate independent contractor status. The appropriate analysis is contextual: assess exclusivity alongside other factors (e.g., control, opportunity for profit or loss, investments, skill and initiative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances and no predetermined weighting of factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic realities test uses a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis; no single factor (including permanence or investment) is dispositive and the Department does not assign predetermined weights to factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply all relevant factors — control, opportunity for profit or loss (including managerial skill), investments (and relative investments), integral (whether the work is integral to the employer's business), and skill and initiative — together. A worker who exhibits business-like indicia (controls conditions of employment, sets fees, hires helpers, markets their services, etc.) will not be deemed an employee solely because one factor (e.g., a long relationship) suggests otherwise. Consider also whether employers have manipulated tenure or permanence to evade FLSA obligations — such concerns are typically enforcement issues for adjudication rather than textual regulation.
